title: Αἴλουρος καὶ ὄρνιθες
part: The Cat and the Birds (Chambry 14 · Perry 7)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 14 (= Perry 7). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Αἴλουρος ἀκούσας ὅτι ἔν τινι ἐπαύλει ὄρνεις νοσοῦσι, σχηματίσας ἑαυτὸν εἰς ἰατρὸν καὶ τὰ τῆς ἐπιστήμης πρόσφορα ἀναλαβὼν ἐργαλεῖα, παρεγένετο, καὶ στὰς πρὸ τῆς ἐπαύλεως ἐπυνθάνετο αὐτῶν πῶς ἔχοιεν.
sentences.tr: Ailouros akousas hoti en tini epaulei orneis nosousi, schēmatisas heauton eis iatron kai ta tēs epistēmēs prosphora analabōn ergaleia, paregeneto, kai stas pro tēs epauleōs epynthaneto autōn pōs echoien.
sentences.l: A cat, having heard that in a certain farmyard the birds were sick, having got himself up as a doctor and having taken up the instruments proper to the art, arrived, and having taken his stand before the farmyard enquired of them how they were.
sentences.i: A cat heard that the hens in a farmyard were ailing, so he got himself up as a doctor, took up the instruments belonging to the profession, and came and stood before the yard and asked them how they did.
sentences.n: Three aorist participles before the main verb (ἀκούσας, σχηματίσας, ἀναλαβών), and a fourth (στάς) after it — the chain at full stretch, and the whole plot of the fable is in it. ὄρνις is “bird” generally and “barnyard fowl” in practice; these are the hens of the ἔπαυλις, the walled steading with its outbuildings. ἐπιστήμη here is the doctor's professional skill, his art, not “science” in the modern sense. τὰ … πρόσφορα … ἐργαλεῖα is split around its genitive τῆς ἐπιστήμης — hyperbaton again. πῶς ἔχοιεν: ἔχω with an adverb means “to be in such a state”, so “how they were doing”, and the optative marks an indirect question after a past verb.

sentences.t: Αἱ δὲ ὑποτυχοῦσαι· « Καλῶς, ἔφασαν, ἐὰν σὺ ἐντεῦθεν ἀπαλλαγῇς. »
sentences.tr: Hai de hypotychousai: « Kalōs, ephasan, ean sy enteuthen apallagēis. »
sentences.l: And they, catching him up: « Well, they said, if you get yourself away from here. »
sentences.i: They took him up at once: « Very well — if you will take yourself off. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχοῦσαι is the participle of ὑποτυγχάνω, “to catch a speaker up”, the standard way of marking a reply broken straight in. Καλῶς is the adverb that answers his πῶς — “well” — and then the condition pulls it away; the verb (“we are”) is left to be understood. The speech-verb ἔφασαν sits inside the quotation, as Greek regularly puts it. ἐάν with the subjunctive (ἀπαλλαγῇς) is the ordinary future condition, “if you do get away”.

sentences.t: Οὕτως καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ πονηροὶ τοὺς φρονίμους οὐ λανθάνουσι, κἂν τὰ μάλιστα χρηστότητα ὑποκρίνωνται.
sentences.tr: Houtōs kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi ponēroi tous phronimous ou lanthanousi, kan ta malista chrēstotēta hypokrinōntai.
sentences.l: So too the wicked among men do not escape the notice of the sensible, even if they act out honesty to the utmost.
sentences.n: This moral opens with οὕτως καί, “so too…”, mapping the story straight onto life, rather than the commoner ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι. λανθάνω takes an accusative of the person kept in the dark: “they do not escape the sensible”. τὰ μάλιστα is an adverbial accusative, “to the utmost”. ὑποκρίνωνται is the actor's verb once more — the same root as the ὑποκρίσεις of the preceding fable.
